hook.text: Every model starts with one sentence: what one row means. One row per order line, or one row per account per month. That sentence is the grain, and the rest of the model is built on it.

plan.text: Twenty-two questions on facts, dimensions and grain. Nine are worked through on real tables in Postgres, and thirteen quick ones close the round.

facts.text: Question one. What are fact and dimension tables? A fact table records events at a declared grain, here one row per order: a key for the order's date, a key for its product, and the amount.

dims.text: Dimension tables hold what you slice by: each date, each product's category. The fact answers how much. The dimensions answer by what.

facts-test.text: So for any new column, ask whether you'd aggregate it or group by it. Aggregate it, and it's a measure on the fact. Group by it, and it belongs on a dimension.

grain.text: Question two. What is the grain, and why pin it down first? The grain is what one row represents. Say it before any column: one row per order line.

grain-test.text: Then every column has to make sense at that grain. Quantity and amount do. A shipping fee doesn't: it's charged once per order, so an order with three lines carries its five dollars three times, and the sum says fifteen.

grain-fix.text: Move it to a fact at order grain, or split it across the lines so the shares add back to five.

grain-why.text: Nothing errors. The total is simply wrong, and a declared grain catches it before anyone sums.

star.text: Question three. Star versus snowflake? In a star, each dimension is one flat table. These twelve products carry their category as text, so Books is written three times.

snow.text: Snowflake it, and category moves to a table of its own, each name stored once. Revenue by category now takes two joins instead of one, and the same six rows come back.

star-pick.text: So the star is the default for business intelligence, or BI, tools: fewer joins to get wrong, and the repeated text costs little. Snowflake a dimension only when it's huge, or genuinely shared.

sk.text: Question four. What is a surrogate key, and why prefer it over a natural key? A natural key comes from the source, like customer ID forty-two. A surrogate key is one the warehouse makes up, and it means nothing.

sk-versions.text: That's what lets customer forty-two have two rows: ten oh one while Acme Corp was in the East, ten oh two once it moved West. Each order matches the version it was placed under.

sk-why.text: Natural keys also change, get reused, or clash when two sources each have a customer forty-two. The natural key stays on the row, so each load can look up which surrogate a new fact gets.

hash.text: Question five. What are the trade-offs of using a hash surrogate key versus a sequence integer? A hash of the natural key is deterministic. The MD5 of forty-two is the same string in development, in production, and in tomorrow's rebuild, so a fact can compute it without a lookup.

hash-size.text: Integers are compact: a hundred thousand integer keys built an index under a third the size of the same number of hashes.

hash-trap.text: But an integer has to be handed out once, by one counter, and kept. Number the rows with row number on every rebuild, and a new customer with a lower ID shifts every key after it. On Monday, Acme was key three. On Tuesday, three is Umbrella, and Monday's order reads as theirs.

hash-pick.text: So hashes suit projects that rebuild often, in many environments, and they're common in dbt, the tool these models are usually built with. They can collide, rarely, so test the key for uniqueness either way.

additive.text: Question six. What is the difference between additive, semi-additive, and non-additive measures? Revenue is additive: it sums across every dimension.

semi.text: A balance is semi-additive. Across accounts on one day, it sums fine: sixteen hundred dollars at the end of March. Across time, it doesn't: the quarter's three month-ends add up to forty-eight hundred, money nobody ever had.

semi-fix.text: Over time, take the closing balance, or the average.

nonadd.text: Non-additive measures, like ratios and distinct counts, sum across nothing. Three users on Monday and three on Tuesday were four people. Recount them from the rows at the grain.

ratio.text: Question seven. Why should you avoid storing percentages or ratios directly in fact tables? Because every roll-up gets them wrong. Take two orders, with margins of fifty and ten percent.

ratio-sum.text: Sum them, and the margin is sixty percent. Average them, and it's thirty. The real margin is fourteen, because the ten percent order carries nine-tenths of the revenue.

ratio-fix.text: So store the additive parts, gross revenue and cost of goods sold, and divide after summing. A ratio of sums weighs each order by its revenue. A stored percentage has forgotten that weight.

role.text: Question eight. What is a role-playing dimension? One physical table used several times by one fact, in different roles. Each order here has three date keys: ordered, shipped and delivered.

role-join.text: So the date dimension is joined three times, under three aliases. Order one oh one was placed on March first, shipped on the third, and delivered on the seventh.

role-why.text: Kept once, it answers what no single role can: order to delivery took six point seven days on average, nine at most.

role-view.text: For BI tools, give each role its own view, with columns named for it, like ship date, so nobody filters on the wrong date.

bridge.text: Question nine. What is a bridge table, and when do you need one? When one fact row relates to several members of a dimension, like an order with two promotions. The fact only has room for one promotion key.

bridge-pairs.text: So a bridge table holds one row per order and promotion, twenty-four pairs for twelve orders, each with a weight.

bridge-fan.text: Join through it and sum the amount, and every order counts once per promotion. Twelve orders worth forty-nine hundred dollars report eleven thousand five hundred five, and nothing looks wrong.

bridge-weight.text: Multiply by the weight first. Each order's weights add up to one, so the promotions share exactly forty-nine hundred.

bridge-touched.text: The unweighted sums still answer one question, how much revenue each promotion touched. Just never total them.

rapid-in.text: Thirteen quick ones, a sentence or two each.

r-types.text: Question ten. What are the three types of fact tables? Transaction: one row per event, like a deposit. Periodic snapshot: one row per entity per period, like a month-end balance. Accumulating snapshot: one row per process, like a loan application, updated in place as each milestone lands.

r-periodic.text: Question eleven. When would you choose a periodic snapshot over a transaction fact? When the question is where things stood. Ben made no transaction in February, and his February balance, five hundred dollars, is still a row.

r-factless.text: Question twelve. What is a factless fact table? Keys and no measures: which products were on promotion in which store, each day. Count rows to answer it, but count what's asked. Store five promoted three products last week, in eleven rows.

r-degen.text: Question thirteen. What is a degenerate dimension? A key with no table behind it, like an order number on the order-line fact. It has nothing to describe, so it stays on the fact, and you still group by it.

r-junk.text: Question fourteen. What is a junk dimension? Small flags, is promo, is gift wrap and is expedited, gathered into one table of every combination: eight rows, and one key on the fact instead of three flags.

r-date.text: Question fifteen. What is the purpose of a date dimension, and what columns does it typically include? One row per day, three hundred sixty-six for 2024, with year, quarter, month, week and weekend worked out once. The columns that matter most are the ones no function knows: holidays and the fiscal calendar.

r-conformed.text: Question sixteen. What is a conformed dimension? One dimension shared by several facts, with the same keys and the same meanings, so their numbers line up.

r-confirmed.text: Question seventeen. What is the difference between a confirmed versus a conformed dimension? It's a vocabulary check: conformed is the term, and confirmed isn't one.

r-drill.text: Question eighteen. What does drilling across mean in dimensional modeling? Combining metrics from two facts, like sales and returns. Roll each fact up to the conformed dimension on its own, then full outer join the results on its key. Joined row to row, the facts would multiply.

r-agg.text: Question nineteen. What is the difference between a fact's grain and its level of aggregation? The grain is the finest detail a fact stores: one row per order. Aggregation is how far a mart rolls it up, here twenty-four orders into six categories. That mart's own grain is one row per category, and the fact keeps every order.

r-bank.text: Question twenty. How would you model a many-to-many relationship between customers and accounts in a bank data warehouse? A bridge between customers and the balance fact, with each owner's share. Unweighted, a joint account counts twice. Weighted, the customers add back to the bank's total.

r-3nf.text: Question twenty-one. What is normalization in third normal form, and why does dimensional modeling deliberately avoid it for dimensions? In third normal form, every column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key, so each fact is stored once. Dimensions break it on purpose, folding category into product, to save joins. The copies stay consistent, because one pipeline writes them.

r-kimball.text: Question twenty-two. How does Kimball's approach differ from Inmon's? Kimball is bottom-up: a star per business process, joined by conformed dimensions, so value comes fast. Inmon is top-down: a normalized enterprise warehouse first, then marts cut from it. It's more consistent, and slower to start.

next.text: Every dimension here held still, except one: customer forty-two already has two rows, because Acme Corp moved. Next: dimensions that change.
